owner: ravenclaude-core (domain-neutral, per AGENTS.md house rule 1 -- no per-agent owner)
review_trigger: weekly researcher-reminder.yml sweep -- ravenclaude-core is already tier_a_news in .ravenclaude/plugins/sweep-tiers.yaml (no new mechanism); re-verify every model_ref against substrate-tier-map.json and model-catalog.json on any sweep that touches either file

sources.note: GitHub Copilot docs (docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/ai-models/supported-models), retrieved 2026-09-01 this build -- no per-Chat model-availability table; Chat inherits its client's (VS Code's) row in the documented per-client table. Copilot CLI and Chat are NOT equivalent for model SELECTABILITY -- see agent-routing-matrix.md.

coding-implementation.label: Writing / editing code -- everyday implementation
coding-implementation.complexity_note: Spans the full interaction-mode range by design: the same content (implementing or changing code) shows up as an inline suggestion, a supervised chat edit, or an autonomous multi-file run. Cheap-lever-tried-first: the default/balanced tier resolves most of it; escalate on demonstrated difficulty, never pre-emptively.

recommendations.quote: Inline completion ⇒ fast/cheap tier only. Latency is the binding constraint; a heavy model here is wasted reasoning, added lag, and added cost
recommendations.rationale: Inline completion is never the place to pay for reasoning depth -- the mode tree gates this at fast/cheap tier unconditionally, before any difficulty judgment.

recommendations.quote: a frontier model on a one-liner wastes latency AND money for no quality gain
recommendations.rationale: Same rule, second host -- the cost tree's FAST leaf names the exact failure mode (frontier on a one-liner) this cell exists to avoid regardless of which CLI is in play.

recommendations.quote: Chat / edit ⇒ balanced default, escalate per task. You are supervising each diff, so the gate is built in; reserve a tier bump for a demonstrably hard sub-task.
recommendations.rationale: The mode tree's chat/edit leaf: you review every diff, so the balanced default is the right standing choice and a tier bump is reserved for a sub-task that proves it needs one.

recommendations.quote: Try the default model first; on Codex raise the reasoning level before upgrading the model - reasoning level costs latency, not dollars
recommendations.rationale: Same cheap-lever-first discipline on the VS Code Copilot Chat surface. Chat's own in-UI model picker is the escalation lever when the balanced default proves insufficient.

recommendations.quote: Agent (autonomous) ⇒ tier follows blast radius, and scope must be defined first. Reversible/PR-opening runs → balanced or raised reasoning
recommendations.rationale: A well-scoped autonomous run that opens a PR is gated by that review, not by a human approving each step -- the mode tree puts this at balanced/raised-reasoning, not frontier.

recommendations.quote: Balanced default tier - best cost-per-resolved-task for most work; measure cost-per-RESOLVED-task, not per-call
recommendations.rationale: Codex's own reasoning-level dial is the cheaper escalation lever before a bigger SKU for a run that turns out harder than expected mid-flight.

Grok Build CLI's balanced tier already carries the architect perspective (SSOT, smallest surface) with high effort -- a reasonable third option for a reversible autonomous run, resolved entirely through the tier map with no independent effort field on this recommendation.

recommendations.quote: AGENT mode with a HUMAN GATE - frontier tier; approval before and at each irreversible step
recommendations.rationale: An irreversible autonomous step (DB writes, deploys, secret rotation, force-push) is never a cost-optimization decision -- the mode tree's rule is unconditional: frontier tier, plus a human gate, no exceptions.

recommendations.quote: irreversible runs → frontier plus a human gate
recommendations.rationale: Same unconditional rule, second host -- an irreversible step never skips the human gate regardless of which CLI is driving it.

coding-debugging-design.label: Hard tail: rare debugging, system design, eval rubrics
coding-debugging-design.complexity_note: Genuine hard tail: the cost of a wrong output exceeds the model premium. Pin frontier for the bounded hard session, then drop back -- never as a standing default. Even hard-tail work starts with cheap triage before it's known to be hard.

recommendations.quote: a frontier model on a one-liner wastes latency AND money for no quality gain
recommendations.rationale: Initial triage of a bug (narrowing a stack trace, a quick syntax fix while investigating) is still latency-bound -- the hard-tail premium applies once the problem is confirmed hard, not to every keystroke along the way.

recommendations.quote: Frontier tier is justified FOR THIS TASK - the cost of a wrong output exceeds the model premium; pin it only for the bounded hard session, then drop back
recommendations.rationale: A rare-debugging or system-design chat session is exactly the cost tree's FRONTIER leaf: the premium is worth it because a wrong answer costs more than the model does. Still chat mode -- you review the output.

An autonomous run tasked with a confirmed-hard bug (not just 'debug this' unscoped) extends the FRONTIER leaf's reasoning to agent mode: pin the premium tier for the bounded hard session, gated by the PR review since the run stays reversible.

recommendations.quote: AGENT mode with a HUMAN GATE - frontier tier; approval before and at each irreversible step
recommendations.rationale: A hard-tail fix that also touches an irreversible surface (e.g. an autonomous fix-and-deploy) compounds two independent frontier-tier triggers -- difficulty and blast radius both point the same direction, with the human gate non-negotiable either way.

recommendations.quote: irreversible runs → frontier plus a human gate
recommendations.rationale: Same compounding logic, second host.

research-deep.label: Multi-source research / fact verification (non-coding)
research-deep.complexity_note: Not a coding task, so no in-repo framework rule names it directly -- routed by extending the same cost-per-resolved-task discipline the coding trees establish, hence basis=cost-heuristic for the class-specific reasoning even where a general framework-rule quote is reused verbatim.

recommendations.rationale: A single fact lookup or quick source check mid-task is latency-bound in the same sense an inline code edit is -- it is not the whole research loop, so it does not warrant the loop's own escalated tiers.
A single research question is everyday work in disguise: the balanced default resolves most of it, escalating only when the question is genuinely contested (multiple disagreeing sources).

A multi-phase, multi-source deep-research run (fan-out search, adversarial verification, synthesis) is the genuine hard tail of research: contested claims need the frontier tier's reconciliation strength during synthesis, even though the per-search-angle phases stay cheap.

recommendations.quote: AGENT mode with a HUMAN GATE - frontier tier; approval before and at each irreversible step
recommendations.rationale: Research becomes irreversible the moment its output is published, sent, or written into a durable knowledge file others will trust -- the mode tree's unconditional gate rule applies regardless of the task's domain.

writing-documentation.label: Long-form writing / documentation (non-coding)
writing-documentation.complexity_note: Structurally close to chat/edit: a human reviews the draft. Balanced default for most writing; escalate for a piece whose stakes justify the premium (a public-facing or legally-reviewed document).

recommendations.rationale: Autocomplete while drafting a sentence is the same latency-bound case as inline code completion -- fast tier, no exceptions for the writing domain.

Drafting prose is a supervised, reversible activity like any other chat/edit work -- the reviewer catches a wrong tone or a factual slip before it ships, so the balanced default is the right standing choice.
A reasonable second option on the same reasoning -- Grok's balanced tier is priced and positioned as the everyday-work rung in the cited lineup, not just for coding tasks.

An autonomous multi-file documentation pass (e.g. updating a whole docs site) that lands as a reviewable PR follows the same reversible-agent rule coding work does: balanced tier, the PR review is the gate.

recommendations.quote: AGENT mode with a HUMAN GATE - frontier tier; approval before and at each irreversible step
recommendations.rationale: Publishing or sending a document autonomously (an email, a public page, a legally-reviewed filing) is an irreversible external action -- the unconditional gate rule applies.

data-analysis.label: Exploratory data analysis / a one-off data question (non-coding)
data-analysis.complexity_note: Usually latency- and cost-sensitive (many small queries) with an occasional genuinely hard reconciliation step (conflicting numbers, an ambiguous methodology) -- mirrors the cost tree's own cheap-lever-then-escalate ladder.

recommendations.rationale: A quick inline query suggestion (autocompleting a filter clause, a column name) is latency-bound the same way an inline code edit is.
Most one-off data questions are everyday work: the balanced default handles a query-and-interpret loop with the human reviewing each result, escalating only when a sub-question proves genuinely hard.

An unsupervised multi-step analysis that must reconcile genuinely conflicting sources or an ambiguous methodology before reporting a conclusion is the hard tail: the frontier tier's reconciliation strength justifies its premium here, same logic as research-deep's agent/reversible cell.

recommendations.quote: AGENT mode with a HUMAN GATE - frontier tier; approval before and at each irreversible step
recommendations.rationale: A data-analysis run that writes back to a production system or triggers a downstream action (not just reads and reports) is irreversible -- the gate rule applies regardless of domain.
